evidence_quotes.quote: The methodological approach of this study involved extensive review of both peer-reviewed and grey literature published from the year 2000–2015.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 5, Section 3.7. Payment for ecosystem services (PES)
evidence_quotes.quote: Water resources can provide the service directly through the water market but also aid other ecosystems in providing their services to the respective markets.

UN Water (2008) approximated that 340 million people were lacking access to safe drinking water; and whether water resources will transform the continent through their effect on human health and labour will depend on the commitment of governments to provide safe drinking water to the populations.

Water resources have been noted to penetrate every interstice of life and to support all sectors of economic growth. However, the way of life in Africa does not reﬂect this kind of wealth in water resources majorly owing to degradation and underutilization of these resources.

criterion_notes.c1: No. The paper is a macro-level thematic overview of natural freshwater resources (lakes, rivers, swamps, aquifers) as drivers of economic sectors across Africa (agriculture, livestock, hydropower, manufacturing, tourism, health, payment for ecosystem services, fisheries, transboundary cooperation and maritime trade), mentioning drinking water and sanitation only in passing via secondary UN reports.
criterion_notes.c2: No under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, and fails overall regardless of reading. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper briefly discusses macro-institutional natural-resource mechanisms—specifically Payment for Ecosystem Services (PES) credits, transboundary river-basin agreements (such as Nile water-sharing treaties) and generic calls for sound national water policies—which concern macro watershed/resource governance rather than household water or sanitation service governance (even if generously treated as touching institutional factors under the plain wording, the study still fails c1, c3, c4 and c5, so plain_criterion2_decision is exclude). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, Criterion 2 is clearly not met because no rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community water/sanitation service access (eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation rules, tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion, enforcement or utility regulatory structure) is examined.
criterion_notes.c3: No. This is a non-systematic narrative review and policy overview synthesizing secondary UN/FAO/UNEP grey reports, websites and literature from 2000–2015 under a conceptual sustainability framework, with no primary empirical data and no systematic empirical synthesis methods (no study eligibility criteria, search flow/counts, extraction or synthesis of empirical studies). Excluded as E05.
criterion_notes.c4: No. The paper reports no empirical outcome measuring household or community water or sanitation access, connection, availability, continuity, quantity, affordability or exclusion, citing only aggregate background figures from secondary UN reports in passing.
criterion_notes.c5: No. As a broad continental narrative review of economic sectors, there is no identifiable empirical population/unit of analysis, legal/administrative exposure or measured service-access outcome.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. Full text is in English.

rationale: Excluded at full text (E05: No empirical evidence; also outside service-access and rule-type mechanism scope). Mugagga and Nabaasa (2016) present a narrative, non-systematic thematic review of secondary reports and online literature on the role of Africa's natural water resources across macro-economic sectors (agriculture, livestock, hydropower, manufacturing, tourism, health, payment for ecosystem services, fisheries, transboundary river cooperation and trade) in achieving the SDGs. It contains no primary empirical data and is not a systematic empirical synthesis, nor does it empirically examine any rule-type legal, administrative or regulatory mechanism governing household or community water or sanitation service access.
